cues.text: A Cautious Churchman
Born in 1917 at Ciudad Barrios, El Salvador, Óscar Romero was ordained a priest in Rome in 1942.
He spent the following decades as a respected but notably conservative churchman — a diligent, traditional pastor and diocesan newspaper editor.
He steered clear of the political engagement increasingly favored by more progressive Latin American clergy of his generation.
An Unexpected Appointment
When Romero was named Archbishop of San Salvador in February 1977, many of El Salvador's ruling elite and conservative Church figures welcomed the choice.
They viewed him as a reliably moderate figure unlikely to challenge either the government or the growing liberation theology movement within the Salvadoran Church.
The Murder That Changed Everything
Just three weeks into his archbishopric, Romero's close friend, the Jesuit priest Rutilio Grande , a vocal advocate for the rural poor, was assassinated by a right-wing death squad.
Romero, deeply shaken, began a dramatic transformation, increasingly speaking out against the escalating violence, repression, and injustice he saw devastating El Salvador's poorest communities.
A Voice for the Voiceless
As El Salvador slid toward civil war, Romero used weekly radio broadcasts of his Sunday homilies to document human rights abuses committed by government forces and allied death squads.
He offered what became known as a 'preferential option for the poor,' making him both beloved among ordinary Salvadorans and intensely hated by the country's military and economic elite.
'Stop the Repression'
In a sermon delivered the day before his death, Romero made a direct and extraordinary appeal to Salvadoran soldiers: "In the name of God, then, in the name of this suffering people...
I beg you, I implore you, I order you in the name of God: stop the repression!"
Legacy
On March 24, 1980, Romero was shot and killed while celebrating Mass in the chapel of a small cancer hospital in San Salvador.
A United Nations truth commission later implicated a right-wing paramilitary leader in orchestrating the assassination, though no one was ever formally prosecuted.
Canonized in 2018 by Pope Francis, Romero is honored as a martyr killed in hatred of the faith.
His witness on behalf of the poor and persecuted remains a defining touchstone for the Church's teaching on justice and human dignity in Latin America and far beyond.
